title: Caritas in Veritate (2009)
hookLine: Benedict XVI: charity in truth, and the place of gift in the economy

lines: A STRANGER PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.
cards: What does a paid-for coffee cost? Most mornings at the counter, everyone ends up square: you pay, they hand you the cup, nobody owes anybody. That's a contract, and it's a fine thing.
But some mornings the person ahead of you pays for yours and walks out before you can say anything. Nothing was owed. Nothing can be paid back.
Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote a letter about the economy, about trade and work and development, and right in the middle of the talk of markets he made room for that second kind of moment.

teach.b: First, the title. Caritas in veritate is Latin for charity in truth. Caritas is the old Church word for the love that gives itself, the word behind the Douay-Rheims line in the first letter of John: "God is charity."
Benedict pairs it with truth on purpose. Love without truth, he warns, slides into sentiment, a warm feeling that can be bent to mean anything. Truth without love turns cold.
He wants them held together, the way Paul writes to the Ephesians: "doing the truth in charity." Second, the economy.

teach.h: THE MARKET AND THE STATE: NEEDED.
teach.b: There's the market, where things are exchanged at an agreed price. There's the state, which shares things out by law. Both, he says, are needed.

teach.h: GIFT BELONGS INSIDE, NOT AT THE EDGE.
teach.b: Third, the gift. Here's the surprising move. Benedict argues that gratuitousness, giving with no return expected, shouldn't be pushed to the edges, to the charity drive after the real work is done.

It should have room within ordinary economic life: in how a business is run, how workers are treated, how a deal is struck. He names this the logic of gift, and roots it in being human: no one made themselves.
Every life is received. Fourth, ordinary life. A shift manager who covers for a worker with a sick child.
A landlord who doesn't raise the rent on the old tenant. A shop with a pay-it-forward board. None of these break the market.
They let something into it that a price can't measure.

teach.h: FREELY HAVE YOU RECEIVED, FREELY GIVE.
teach.b: Jesus says it plainly when he sends out his disciples: "Freely have you received, freely give."

how: Catholics study Caritas in Veritate in parish and university courses on social teaching, and some Catholic business owners point to its logic of gift when shaping how they treat workers and customers.

o: a Latin motto on the Vatican's coins
Benedict XVI's letter: charity in truth
the creed's line on faith and reason

games.q: charity in truth — tap the pairs.

s: Benedict says gift belongs only in charity drives, after the real work
he argues gratuitousness should have room within ordinary economic life itself.
Benedict says the market and the state are both needed
needed, he says, but neither is enough on its own.
the title pairs charity with truth on purpose
love without truth turns to sentiment; truth without love turns cold.

games.q: you run a small business. a worker's child is sick, and the contract says unpaid leave. what does Benedict's letter push you toward?
o: follow the contract exactly; that's fair.
close the business; markets are the problem.
keep the contract, and let some gift into it.
games.why: Benedict doesn't throw out contracts or markets. he asks that the logic of gift find room inside them, in how people are actually treated.

practice: Picture the people you'll pay tomorrow, the ones who'll serve you, the ones you work beside, and find one moment where you could give something nobody is owed: time, a better tip, a covered shift, a word of thanks with a name in it.
Choose one where you won't be thanked, or won't be there to see it. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, simply hold the choice quietly.

wordCard.voice: Caritas in Veritate. Charity in truth: Benedict the Sixteenth's letter on the economy, which makes room for gift alongside contract and law. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: charity in truth, the opening words that give the letter its name.

carryVoice: Your line: the logic of gift. Nothing owed, nothing paid back. That's today, done.
